body:
Bose's place in the national movement

Subhas Chandra Bose was a prominent leader of the Indian National Congress who advocated complete independence from British rule. He believed that India should prepare for a decisive struggle against colonialism and that political freedom should be accompanied by economic planning and social reform.

Bose belonged to the more radical current of Indian nationalism. He favoured strong mass mobilisation and, eventually, the use of armed struggle with international assistance. Mahatma Gandhi, by contrast, regarded non-violence as the essential basis of the national struggle. Both sought Indian independence, but they differed over the methods and timing of the struggle.

These differences became especially important when Europe moved towards the Second World War. Bose wanted Congress to use Britain's growing international difficulties to press immediately for complete independence. Gandhi and several senior Congress leaders did not accept his proposed course of action.

The Haripura Congress session, 1938

In February 1938, Bose presided over the annual session of the Indian National Congress at Haripura, in present-day Surat district, Gujarat. This is an important Gujarat connection in the history of the national movement.

As Congress president, Bose emphasised industrial development, scientific progress and economic planning. During his presidency, the Congress established a National Planning Committee, with Jawaharlal Nehru as its chairman.

The Haripura session is associated with Bose's first term as Congress president. It must not be confused with the Tripuri session of 1939, which became the centre of his conflict with the Congress leadership.

The Tripuri crisis, 1939

Bose sought a second term as Congress president in 1939. He defeated Pattabhi Sitaramayya, whose candidature was supported by Gandhi. Bose's electoral victory did not, however, settle the disagreement over the Congress programme.

At the Tripuri session in March 1939, Bose advocated giving the British government a time-bound demand for independence and preparing a nationwide struggle if it was rejected. Senior leaders disagreed with this approach. The dispute also made it difficult for Bose to form a Congress Working Committee that would support his programme.

Consequently, Bose resigned from the Congress presidency in April 1939. His resignation followed political and organisational disagreements; it was not a result of losing the presidential election.

Formation of the Forward Bloc

In May 1939, Bose announced the formation of the Forward Bloc. It was initially conceived as a grouping within the Congress to bring together radical and left-wing elements and press for a more determined anti-colonial struggle.

The Forward Bloc was a political organisation. It was not the Indian National Army, which developed later in Southeast Asia during the Second World War. In August 1939, the Congress leadership barred Bose from holding elective Congress office for 3 years, deepening the separation.

Prelims focus

  • Haripura, Gujarat, 1938: Bose presided over the Congress session.
  • National Planning Committee: Established during Bose's presidency, with Jawaharlal Nehru as chairman.
  • Tripuri, 1939: Bose's second presidential term became marked by conflict within Congress.
  • Pattabhi Sitaramayya: Defeated by Bose in the 1939 Congress presidential election.
  • April 1939: Bose resigned as Congress president.
  • May 1939: Bose formed the Forward Bloc, initially within Congress.
  • Trap: Bose won the 1939 presidential election; he resigned later because of disagreements over policy and the Working Committee.

[Sources: NCERT, India and the Contemporary World–II, Class 10, chapter 'Nationalism in India', printed pp. 62–63, consulted in the GPSC Books compendium; Lok Sabha Secretariat, Subhas Chandra Bose: A Profile, 2006, sections 'A Dynamic Congress President' and 'Congress President for the Second Term'; Indian National Congress, 'Subhas Chandra Bose as Congress President', passages on Haripura and Tripuri, consulted 22 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: The 1938 Haripura Congress session in Gujarat.

title: Subhas Chandra Bose in Congress: Haripura, Tripuri and the Forward Bloc

body:
Why an Indian army emerged outside India

During the Second World War, Britain fought against the Axis powers, including Japan. Many Indian soldiers served in the British Indian Army. When Japanese forces defeated British forces in parts of Southeast Asia, large numbers of Indian soldiers became prisoners of war.

Some Indian nationalists in Southeast Asia believed that these soldiers, together with Indians living abroad, could form a force to fight British colonial rule. This gave rise to the Indian National Army (INA), also known as the Azad Hind Fauj.

Indian National Army

The INA was a military force organised by Indian nationalists in Southeast Asia during the Second World War to seek India's independence from British rule through armed struggle, with Japanese assistance.

Bose's escape from India

After his conflict with Congress, Bose remained active in anti-colonial politics and was placed under British restrictions. In January 1941, he secretly escaped from his residence in Calcutta.

He travelled through northwestern India and Afghanistan and eventually reached Germany. His purpose was to obtain international support for India's struggle against British rule. He later travelled from Europe to Japanese-controlled Southeast Asia, reaching Singapore in July 1943.

The escape and overseas journey explain how Bose became associated with an Indian military movement outside British-controlled India. They do not mark the original formation of the INA.

The first INA and the Indian Independence League

The first INA was organised in 1942, before Bose arrived in Southeast Asia. Captain Mohan Singh, a former officer of the British Indian Army, was its first major military organiser and commander.

The Indian Independence League (IIL) was a political organisation of Indians in Southeast Asia that supported the struggle for independence. Rash Behari Bose, an Indian revolutionary living in Japan, played a leading role in organising and coordinating this movement.

The first INA drew heavily on Indian prisoners of war captured by Japanese forces. Its development was troubled by disagreements concerning Japanese control and the independence of Indian military leadership. This first organisation weakened and effectively broke down towards the end of 1942.

Subhas Chandra Bose takes charge, 1943

When Subhas Chandra Bose arrived in Singapore in July 1943, Rash Behari Bose transferred leadership of the Indian independence movement in Southeast Asia to him. Subhas then reorganised and expanded the INA.

He sought recruits from former Indian prisoners of war and from Indian communities living in Southeast Asia. His leadership gave the movement a clearer political aim: to enter India, challenge British authority and establish an independent Indian government.

Three names must therefore be distinguished:

  • Captain Mohan Singh: Principal organiser and military commander of the first INA in 1942.
  • Rash Behari Bose: Senior revolutionary who led the Indian Independence League and helped prepare the movement in Southeast Asia.
  • Subhas Chandra Bose: Nationalist leader who assumed leadership in July 1943 and reorganised the INA for the subsequent campaign.

Political movement and military force

The Indian Independence League and the INA were related but distinct. The League organised political support among overseas Indians; the INA was the armed force. Bose later established the Provisional Government of Azad Hind, a separate political institution that claimed to represent an independent India.

Although the INA fought for Indian independence, its wartime activities depended heavily on Japanese assistance. It should not be confused with the British Indian Army, which continued to serve under British command during the war.

Prelims focus

  • January 1941: Subhas Chandra Bose escaped from British surveillance in Calcutta.
  • 1942: The first INA was organised under Captain Mohan Singh.
  • Rash Behari Bose: Associated with the Indian Independence League and the transfer of leadership to Subhas.
  • July 1943: Subhas Chandra Bose assumed leadership of the movement in Southeast Asia.
  • Singapore: A principal centre of Bose's INA organisation.
  • Trap: Subhas Chandra Bose reorganised and led the INA; he did not originally establish the first INA in 1942.

[Sources: Ministry of Home Affairs, Government of India, List of Movements Recognized for Grant of Swatantrata Sainik Samman Pension, entry 18, 'Indian National Army and Indian Independence League (1942 to 1946)'; Lok Sabha Secretariat, Subhas Chandra Bose: A Profile, 2006, section 'His escape from India and foundation of Indian National Army'; NCERT, Our Pasts–III, Class 8, chapter 'The Making of the National Movement: 1870s–1947', printed p. 123, consulted in the GPSC Books compendium; sources consulted 22 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: The IIL was linked to Rash Behari Bose, the first INA to Mohan Singh, and the reorganised INA to Subhas Chandra Bose after July 1943.
pictures.caption: Organisations and leaders of the INA movement.

title: The Formation of the Indian National Army and Bose's Leadership

body:
The Provisional Government of Azad Hind

On 21 October 1943, Subhas Chandra Bose proclaimed the Provisional Government of Azad Hind in Singapore. The expression 'provisional government' means a government established on a temporary basis while claiming authority for a future or contested political order.

The Azad Hind government asserted India's right to independence. Bose headed this government, while the INA served as its principal military force. Its existence did not mean that British rule over India had already ended: the government operated outside the territory effectively controlled by the British Indian administration and depended on support from Japan and its allies.

The political government and the army worked towards the same declared objective, but they were not identical institutions.

The Rani of Jhansi Regiment

A notable feature of Bose's reorganised INA was the establishment of an all-women military unit called the Rani of Jhansi Regiment, named after Rani Lakshmibai of Jhansi.

The regiment was led by Captain Lakshmi Swaminathan, later widely known as Lakshmi Sahgal. Women of Indian origin living in Southeast Asia volunteered for the unit. Its training camp was formally opened in Singapore in October 1943.

The regiment represented an attempt to include women directly in the military organisation of the independence movement. Its members performed training, medical and other wartime duties. The regiment's existence should not be taken to mean that every member fought on the front line in the 1944 Indian campaign.

The call to march towards India

Bose used slogans to communicate the INA's objective and build morale. 'Delhi Chalo' expressed the aim of advancing towards the centre of British authority in India. 'Jai Hind' became closely associated with Bose and the INA as a patriotic greeting and rallying expression.

The INA operated alongside Japanese forces in Southeast Asia and Burma, now Myanmar. Its intended advance into India became closely connected with the Japanese offensive towards the northeastern frontier.

The Imphal and Kohima campaigns

In 1944, Japanese forces and units of the INA advanced towards British-held India from Burma. The major fighting centred on Imphal in Manipur and Kohima in the Naga Hills.

These places are important because they were part of the northeastern approaches to British India. The Japanese-led offensive attempted to weaken Allied control in the region and create an opportunity for an advance into India.

At Moirang in Manipur, INA personnel hoisted the INA flag on 14 April 1944. This was an important symbolic achievement on Indian soil. It did not mean that the INA had secured control of Imphal, Kohima or the rest of northeastern India.

Why the offensive failed

The attempt to enter and hold Indian territory did not succeed. The Japanese-led forces encountered strong Allied resistance. Difficult terrain, monsoon conditions, inadequate supplies and Allied air superiority seriously affected their operations.

The Allied defence of Imphal and Kohima succeeded, and the Japanese-led forces retreated. As Japan's wider position in the Second World War deteriorated, the INA also lost the military support necessary to continue its campaign. By 1945, the INA's military effort had collapsed.

It is therefore necessary to separate the INA's military outcome from its political impact. The campaign failed to defeat British forces, but the INA later became the focus of major nationalist demonstrations when its officers were put on trial.

Prelims focus

  • 21 October 1943: Provisional Government of Azad Hind proclaimed in Singapore.
  • Rani of Jhansi Regiment: Women's unit of the INA led by Captain Lakshmi Swaminathan, later Lakshmi Sahgal.
  • Delhi Chalo: Slogan associated with the INA's intended advance towards India.
  • 1944: INA participated in the Japanese-led campaign towards Imphal and Kohima.
  • 14 April 1944: INA flag hoisted at Moirang, Manipur.
  • Trap: The flag-hoisting at Moirang was significant, but the Imphal–Kohima offensive ultimately failed.

[Sources: Lok Sabha Secretariat, Subhas Chandra Bose: A Profile, 2006, section on the Indian National Army and Azad Hind; Ministry of Home Affairs, Government of India, List of Movements Recognized for Grant of Swatantrata Sainik Samman Pension, entries 2, 3 and 18; Archives of Contemporary India, Ashoka University, 'Lakshmi Sahgal Papers (1946–2010)', biographical and collection description; Ministry of Culture, Government of India, press information on Moirang, issued 2021; NCERT, Our Pasts–III, Class 8, chapter 'The Making of the National Movement: 1870s–1947', printed p. 123; online sources consulted 22 November 2026.]
